findings.where: The pad ground across the whole page: the horizontal feints and the double margin line, at both widths, compared with the Palette swatches (Feint #93B3D3, Margin red #B8322B) and the Texture sample
findings.fault: On the page itself the ruled lines look olive-grey and the double margin line looks dark brown. The palette names those lines as pale blue feints and a red margin, and the Texture sample's own lines do show pale blue. Pale blue rules and a red double margin are what make a sheet read as a legal pad. Without them the ground reads as generic khaki lined paper, and the tile's swatches disagree with the page they claim to describe.
findings.who_objects: Mark chose the legal pad 'given my legal background', and the blue feint and red margin are what he would recognise. The layout round would object too, since it builds from the swatches and would get a ground that doesn't match what this page shows.

findings.where: Motion sketch, the timeline table (Element / Start / Length / Easing) and its row dividers, at both widths; also the photo caption in the hero
findings.fault: The table is set at a smaller size on a tighter leading than the page's 32 px feint, so its lines drift off the rules and the pad's feints run through and under the words. Its own row dividers add a second set of horizontal lines that don't line up with the feints. The page's own Texture note says the feints are 'the line spacing of every text block', and this block breaks that.
findings.who_objects: A reader of the table sees words crossed by ruled lines and two kinds of rule tangled together. Angélique, adding a post that holds a table, would get the same collision, since this is the only specimen that shows how dense text sits on the pad.

findings.where: Article specimen, the attached-document row ('Streamlining the PPP Process… · Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF'), at both widths
findings.fault: The row's bottom divider, in full ink, sits a pixel or two under the title's link underline. Under '‘Abundance’ Challenge' the two lines merge into one heavy double rule, and the divider also cuts close under '2026 · PDF'. The link mark and the row edge become one blurred line instead of two distinct marks.
findings.who_objects: A reader scanning for the document can't tell where the underline ends and the box edge begins. Up close it looks like a rendering slip, which matters on the one specimen a lay editor will copy for every PDF Mark posts.

findings.where: Motion sketch panel border against its 'Replay the sketch' button, at both widths
findings.fault: The static motion-sketch panel is outlined in full ballpoint ink at the same weight and colour as the outline of the Replay button inside it. The only other framed specimen, the Texture sample, uses a pale feint edge. A static panel and a control therefore share one edge treatment, and the two framed specimens are treated differently from each other.
findings.who_objects: A visitor reads the dark ink box as something to act on, as the button is, so the one real control in it stands out less. The layout round would get two conflicting edge treatments for the same kind of framed panel.

findings.where: The page edge at desktop width: the Pad sheet (#F6E68A) against the Under-sheet band (#EED96C) on either side
findings.fault: The pad and the under-sheet are two large yellow grounds sharing an edge, and they are only slightly different, by roughly ΔE00 4. That is in the house's near-miss zone. They don't read as a stack of sheets, more as a faint mismatch in the background yellow, and only the soft shadow separates them.
findings.who_objects: A desktop visitor sees a slightly off yellow strip down each side that looks like a fill error rather than paper underneath. The house palette rule asks for the same colour or a clearly different one.
